blocks.text: Create a Commute If You Work from Home!
Fake it! Photo by Tom Sodoge on Unsplash Throughout my early twenties, I worked in the hospitality industry.

Sometimes it was part-time while juggling classes, and other times, it was a full-time job—serving drinks behind a bar, managing front-of-house, and learning how to keep a cool head when the lines outside stretched past midnight.
My daily grind was predictable: early wake-up, commute in the dark through the city, shift end followed by a hurried rush home before the weekend hit.
Then, like so many, I pivoted to remote work.
No more rushing through rain-soaked streets or enduring slow subway trains.
Instead, my morning routine became as simple as rolling out of bed and hitting “on” at my desk.
My commute? Gone. My daily ritual?
Suddenly, it had to be invented.
At first, I reveled in the freedom—baked pastries for breakfast, lazy lunches, late-night work with no traffic to complain about.
But, as I tell friends who still clock in on buses and in cubicles, I realized there’s a hidden cost to ditching the commute.
Let’s face it: not having a commute is a gift.
But if you’re like me and you *miss* it—or maybe you’re tempted to hang on to the old routine out of habit—you can create your own commute, even if you’re already at your desk.
A “commute” isn’t just about leaving your house; it’s about the ritual, the transition, the psychological shift from “home” to “work mode.” Start with a physical boundary.

blocks.text: Pictured with the Founders of TokenFest and four phenomenal women in blockchain, I’ve had the rare opportunity to immerse myself in the pulsating heart of San Francisco’s Crypto and Blockchain scene.
The buzz is impossible to ignore; from buzzing startup incubators to star-studded panels, it’s clear that the world of Crypto and Blockchain is not slowing down—it’s exploding.
For those curious about diving into this fascinating (and sometimes bewildering) world, here are 15 tips to help you get started on the right foot.
1. **Start with the Basics:** You don’t need to be a coder to understand Crypto and Blockchain.
Grasp the fundamental concepts—like decentralization, hash functions, and public/private key cryptography.
There are fantastic free resources online, like Crypto.co and Crypto.com’s learn hubs.
2. **Follow Reputable News Outlets:** Platforms like CoinDesk, The Block, and CoinTelegraph offer timely and well-researched coverage.
Bookmark a few, and make it a habit to check them daily to stay up-to-date.
3. **Join Online Communities:** Reddit’s r/CryptoCurrency and r/Blockchain, along with Discord and Telegram channels, are full of passionate newcomers and experts.
Participating respectfully can help you learn a lot and find mentors.
4. ** attend Local Events and Meetups:** Even if you’re not in San Francisco, most cities have or host events like webinars, panels, and hackathons.

blocks.text: The ultimate question most people have in life is, “what should I do?” This question, deceptively simple yet overwhelmingly complex, often gets translated into something more concrete: “What kind of profession do I want?” or “What kind of life do I want to lead?” We grow up hearing that our careers will define us, that our jobs are the lynchpins of our happiness and success.
The schoolsystem and society steer us toward certain paths, subtly (and sometimes not so subtly) nudging us to choose a “viable” future.
But here’s the thing: the real question might be broader—or, more accurately, more fluid than we’re taught to imagine.
It’s not *just* about what job to take or the title on our resume.
It’s about aligning our daily actions, passions, values, and desires with a life that feels meaningful, sustainable, and authentic.

Most people I know spend years analyzing job descriptions, networking, and quizzing mentors about what “looks good on paper.” But if pressed, if really pressed, the question that matters most isn’t whether I’ll earn a living doing X, but whether living that X every day will leave me feeling fulfilled, not just for now but for the long run.
It’s easy to fall into the trap of thinking our futures are predestined.
We’re told to become doctors, engineers, teachers, lawyers—a “safe” path that promises stability and respect.
But what if the answer isn’t among those options?
What if the life we’re truly meant to build lies outside the textbook?

blocks.text: Life is anything but predictable.
People will argue the validity of free will until the end of time.
One thing remains to be true though.
So much of life boils down to how you react to it.
I like to think that being proactive is more than just showing up on time or packing for the weather.
But yet, time itself—our most intangible resource—reveals more about our character than we often realize.
Punctuality, that oft-maligned trait, is actually a quiet mirror reflecting far deeper parts of ourselves than mere responsibility.
And in the chaos of modern life, where meetings are moved at the last minute and plans unravel daily, your punctuality might say a lot about who you are in a world that rarely rewards consistency.
First, let’s face it: punctuality isn’t just about respect for others’ time.
For those who are chronically late, it’s rarely a simple matter of forgetting an alarm or overestimating traffic.
More often, it’s a symptom of underlying habits or mental patterns—the kind that affect everything from work to relationships to self-trust.
Consistently arriving late can reflect an underestimation of your own priorities, or an overestimation of the time you have.
It might also signal unresolved anxiety or difficulty with structure, especially in an era where unpredictability feels the norm.
But punctuality is even more telling when considered from the perspective of the punctual person.
To show up early, ready to go and to wait patiently when others are not, is an act of faith in systems, in humanity, and in yourself.
It’s not just helpful; it’s considerate.

blocks.text: “The major impact of this theory [pragmatism] is to shift talk about truth to talk about knowledge, and talk about knowledge to talk about the achievements of human powers and practices.

As William James so aptly observed, pragmatism does not rest its hopes on the immutable stone of absolute truth, but rather on the provisional and practical results of our endeavors—our experiments, our inventions, our conversations.
In this light, the virtue of muddling through is not only accepted, but celebrated as an essential part of progress.

Traditionally, Western thought has clung to notions of truth as an absolute, unchanging target—something out there in the universe that we could, in principle, reach if only we were smart or sincere enough.
Pragmatism, by contrast, argues that truth is what works, what is useful, what leads to better outcomes or resolutions for real-world problems.

It asks not ‘Is this true?’ but ‘What difference, if any, does this make?’ If a claim fails to produce practical results or if it cannot be tested or imagined in useful ways, it is treated as epistemically suspect—or not knowledge at all.
And here, we find the unexpected nobility in ‘muddling through.’ Pragmatism does not demand clarity before action.
Instead, it recognizes that human knowledge is built incrementally, through trial, error, and adaptation.
We do not have all the answers from the start.
Our best theories today are often rough drafts, provisional hypotheses, or workarounds for the difficulties we’ve yet to understand.
To ‘muddle through’ is thus not a failure, but a method.
It is the courage to act in the face of uncertainty, the willingness to refine our thinking as we go, and the humility to admit that we don’t yet know enough to be certain.

blocks.text: Zion National Park in Utah. Picture taken by yours truly Learning how to love myself through creative writing has been a journey I wish I’d begun sooner.
Every time I sit down with a blank page, I find myself peeling back the layers of self-doubt, guilt, and silence that I’d kept wrapped like old photographs in a drawer.
As I translate my thoughts into words—no filter, just honesty—my inner voice grows louder and clearer.
The act of articulating my feelings, needs, and dreams is like pressing a reset button for my self-worth.
At first, I imagined writing as a way to impress or persuade others.
But as the words flowed, I realized it was less about “audience” and more about dialogue with myself.
Through poetry, stories, and even journaling, I discovered the courage to acknowledge things I had avoided: my anxieties, my frustrations, my small victories.
And in that honest conversation, I began to see myself not as a flawed figure, but as a whole person navigating a complex, beautiful landscape.
It wasn’t always comfortable. There were days the narrative felt harsh, unrelenting, unkind.
But the more I wrote, the more I learned to hold that narrative gently, to critique it without anger, to empathize with my own struggles.
Gradually, the voice that once whispered, “You’re not enough,” began to echo, “You are learning.
You are growing. You are enough, in this moment.” This journey of self-advocacy through writing means standing up and claiming my truth.
It’s about recognizing my own value even when it feels invisible.
It’s about crafting my own story—not to fit anyone else’s mold, but to discover my own.

blocks.text: Illustration by Fresh Idea Full manuscript in two months.
That was the goal. I was on vacation in Mexico, no less, when I checked my email and saw the opportunity.
It was mid-June and the conference was happening near the coast—just a quick hop by flight for someone willing to hustle.
I’d already sketched an outline in my head during an espresso binge.
The idea felt exciting, manageable… until the ego got in the way.
It’s easy to lose sight of how much our egos masquerade as motivation.
Mine, at least, had developed a habit of flexing whenever I sensed potential success.
Instead of diving into the quiet grind, I started second-guessing my outline.
“Is this outline too simple?” I fretted, scrolling Pinterest for more visually stunning inspiration that would “elevate” my manuscript.
“If the other presenters have graphs, I should add some graphs,” I reasoned—spending hours hunting for infographics that, frankly, didn’t belong in my work.
Then, when actual writing began, my inner critic took over.
“Is this sentence clear enough?” “Are these characters compelling enough?” Each time a line felt imperfect, my mind rewritten it until it lost its original spark.
Every paragraph was a negotiation between my authentic voice and what I thought the academic audience wanted to hear.
The result? Stasis. A document that kept growing longer—and losing substance.
I realized too late that my ego wasn’t helping me write; it was preventing me from writing.

blocks.text: I don’t consider myself a Buddhist, but I recite what are called the “three refuges” after meditating each morning.

I even have them tattooed on my arm along with a fourth: “Buddha, dharma, sangha.” Maybe it sounds a bit cliché, but when the world feels like it’s spiraling into chaos—especially during the coronavirus outbreak—these words anchor me.
In the morning, as sunlight filters through my window and the world outside blurs into a swirl of news and panic, I close my eyes and quietly repeat: “I take refuge in Buddha.
I take refuge in the dharma. I take refuge in the sangha.” The words, which originated centuries ago as a simple declaration of faith and community, now feel like a lifeline.
Buddhism, in its purest sense, is about finding balance within the storm.
It doesn’t promise us that things will get easier overnight; instead, it teaches us to look at suffering, uncertainty, and fear without being consumed by them.
When the world feels unbearably heavy—as it does during a global pandemic—the practice of mindfulness, often associated with Buddhist meditation, becomes my personal toolkit.
Through daily meditation, I learn to observe my thoughts rather than get swept away by them.
Instead of wrestling with “why me?” or “this is unfair,” I simply notice the anxiety rising, see it as a passing cloud, and let it drift.
It isn’t about suppressing emotions but learning to sit with them, like watching waves roll ashore instead of being tossed by them.
Perhaps even more valuable has been the dharma—the teachings.
The Buddha didn’t offer easy answers or miracle cures.
